fixes.answer: Not at all, and this is a common misconception. While peer pressure is usually associated with negative behaviour, it can be a powerful positive force too. If your peers are ambitious and disciplined, their influence can motivate you to raise your own standards. So peer pressure is really a [[double-edged sword]]; its effect depends entirely on [[the company you keep]] and how [[discerning]] you are.
fixes.why: 'motivate' is plain; marked 'double-edged sword' and the idiom 'the company you keep'

fixes.answer: During the teenage years specifically, I would argue friends often have the greater immediate influence. Adolescents are forming their own identity and naturally seek acceptance from their peers, sometimes [[at the expense of]] parental advice. However, parents provide the deeper, [[underlying]] values that tend to [[resurface]] later in life. So peers shape day-to-day behaviour, while parents shape long-term character.
fixes.why: 'character' is plain; marked 'at the expense of'

fixes.answer: It largely comes down to their [[developmental stage]]. Adolescents have a deep psychological need to belong and fear social rejection intensely. Their sense of identity is still forming, which makes them more [[susceptible]] to conforming with the group. Additionally, the part of the brain governing [[impulse control]] is not yet fully developed, so they are more likely to act on that pressure.
fixes.why: 'belong' and 'pressure' are plain; marked 'developmental stage' and 'impulse control'

fixes.answer: The desire to fit in is an extraordinarily powerful driver of behaviour. It can lead people to [[conform]] to group norms even when they privately disagree, a phenomenon that affects everything from fashion to opinions. While this social [[cohesion]] has its benefits, it can also [[suppress individuality]] and lead to poor decisions. Learning to resist this pull and think independently is a mark of real maturity.

Absolutely, I think it has intensified it dramatically. In the past, peer pressure was confined to your immediate social circle, but now it is constant and global. People compare themselves to countless others online, and the pressure to project a perfect image is [[relentless]]. This [[amplified]], round-the-clock pressure is, I believe, [[taking a serious toll]] on young people's wellbeing.
fixes.why: 'wellbeing' is plain; marked 'taking a serious toll'

fixes.answer: Building self-confidence is the most effective safeguard. A young person with a strong sense of self is far less likely to [[succumb]] to pressure. Parents and teachers can help by fostering open communication, so children feel able to discuss difficult situations. Teaching practical strategies, like how to say no gracefully, also [[empowers]] them to [[stand firm]].

On the positive side, wanting to [[emulate]] others can inspire self-improvement; admiring successful people can push us to work harder. It also helps social [[integration]]. The negative side is that it can lead to a loss of individuality and constant, unhealthy comparison. It may cause people to suppress their true selves to fit in. The healthiest approach is to draw inspiration from others while [[staying true to]] who you are.
fixes.why: 'inspiration' is plain and 'suppress' now marked in Q4; marked 'emulate' and 'staying true to'
